passage:
Last Diwali was my first at Jaya's house, though we've lived three buildings apart for years. I was nervous the whole way. What if I did something wrong? I'd bought a box of kaju katli from the corner shop, and I took my shoes off outside the door without being told. During the Lakshmi puja I stood at the back with folded hands. I didn't pray the way they did; I just watched the lamps and noticed how quiet the room felt. Jaya's father handed me prasad and said, 'You came. That's enough.' This Eid, her whole family came to ours, and Ammi made sheer khurma. Strange how one box of sweets can open two doors.
Imran

qa.q: What did Imran bring to Jaya's house?
qa.a: A box of kaju katli.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling on the way to the first Diwali visit?
qa.a: Imran felt nervous, worried about doing something wrong in a home with different customs.

qa.q: Which of Imran's actions showed respect without sharing the beliefs?
qa.a: Bringing sweets, taking off shoes at the door, and standing quietly with folded hands at the back during the puja.

qa.q: How did Jaya's father seem to see Imran's visit?
qa.a: He seemed touched and welcoming, telling Imran that simply coming was enough.

grounding: Shows a young adult who visits a friend's home on their festival with sweets and respects their customs without sharing the beliefs, building trust between neighbours.

Society newsletter jotting, December. Gautam, secretary.
At the D'Costa family's Christmas open house, I noticed Simran from B-wing, twenty-four, arrive with a tray of pinnis she had made herself. She stood quietly during the grace before dinner, head slightly bowed, then helped Mrs. D'Costa hand out cake to the children. When little Joel asked if she believed in Santa, she laughed and said she believed in cake. In January the D'Costas turned up at Simran's family's Gurpurab langar with a basket of oranges. Next year I plan to put both dates on the society calendar, so everyone knows whose door is open when.

qa.q: What did Simran bring to the Christmas open house?
qa.a: A tray of pinnis she had made herself.

qa.q: What does Simran's joke about believing in cake suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relaxed and happy there, comfortable sharing the joy without needing to share the beliefs.

qa.q: What is Gautam's plan, and why could it help the society?
qa.a: Putting both families' festival dates on the society calendar, so neighbours know they are welcome and more visits across faiths happen.

qa.q: How might the D'Costa family have felt about Simran's visit?
qa.a: They likely felt respected and warmly connected, which is why they came to her family's Gurpurab langar in return.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who joins a neighbour's festival with homemade sweets and respects their customs without sharing the beliefs, and the trust it builds in a mixed neighbourhood.

passage:
Monday, Eid night.

Went to Rizwan's for Eid with Sumit from office. I was nervous on the way: do I say Eid Mubarak with a hug? Do I take off my shoes? What if I do something wrong?

We took a box of kaju katli from the old sweet shop. Rizwan's Ammi opened the door, and before I could decide anything, Rizwan hugged us both, three times, the proper way, laughing at how stiff I was.

Sheer khurma, biryani, and his Nani asking whether I was married yet. (No, Nani.) When the family went to the next room to pray, Sumit and I sat quietly in the drawing room with his little nephew, who showed us his new watch.

On the way out, Ammi packed us each a box. Rizwan said, "Diwali, I'm coming to yours. Your mother's chakli."

Happy tired. Glad we went.

Siddharth

qa.q: What did Siddharth and Sumit bring?
qa.a: They took a box of kaju katli from the old sweet shop.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling on the way to Rizwan's house?
qa.a: Siddharth felt nervous and unsure about the customs, worried about doing something wrong.

qa.q: What did Siddharth and Sumit do that showed respect?
qa.a: They brought sweets, followed the family's lead on greetings, and sat quietly with the nephew while the family prayed, without needing to share the beliefs.

qa.q: How does Rizwan see the visit?
qa.a: Rizwan is delighted, hugging them warmly and inviting himself for Diwali, which shows growing trust.

grounding: Shows a young adult visiting a friend's home on Eid, bringing sweets and respecting the customs without sharing the beliefs, building trust.

passage:
In the small town near Nagpur, Nilesh's family always celebrated Buddha Purnima at the vihara at the end of their lane, and this year Nilesh had asked Tarun to come.

Tarun brought a box of pedhas from the station sweet shop and wore his best white shirt. At the vihara he took off his shoes, sat cross-legged on the mat beside Nilesh's father, and stayed silent through the chanting, watching the lamps float in the brass bowl.

Afterwards, Nilesh's aunt served kheer to everyone in the lane, whatever their faith. The old man from the flour mill clapped Tarun on the back. "You came for our festival? Good boy."

Walking home, Nilesh said, "You didn't have to sit through all that."

"I wanted to see what matters to you," Tarun said. "Now come for Ganpati. Aai's making modaks."

qa.q: What did Tarun bring?
qa.a: Tarun brought a box of pedhas from the station sweet shop.

qa.q: What does Tarun's 'I wanted to see what matters to you' show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows warmth and respect for Nilesh; he cared about his friend's festival without needing to share the belief.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's actions showed respect for the customs?
qa.a: Taking off his shoes, sitting quietly through the chanting, and bringing sweets, then inviting Nilesh back for Ganpati.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's family see Tarun's visit?
qa.a: They likely feel honoured and more trusting, like the old man who clapped him on the back.

grounding: Shows a young adult joining a friend's festival at the vihara, bringing sweets and respecting the customs without sharing the beliefs.

passage:
On the first night of Hanukkah, Abebe, twenty-five, stood outside Noa's family flat in Haifa, holding a box of sufganiyot from the kosher bakery on the corner. He had asked Noa beforehand what he could bring, and whether he should cover his head. He was Ethiopian Orthodox and had never been to a Jewish home for a festival.
Noa's grandfather lit the first candle and sang a blessing. Abebe stood quietly, hands folded, not joining the words but watching carefully. Noa's little brother showed him how to spin the dreidel, and Abebe lost every round, laughing. Noa's mother said, "You're the first of Noa's colleagues to ask about our customs before coming." Abebe said, "You came to our Timket last year, remember? I owed you." As he left, the grandfather pressed his hand. "Come on the eighth night too." Abebe said he would.

qa.q: What did Abebe bring to Noa's family?
qa.a: A box of sufganiyot from the kosher bakery on the corner.

qa.q: How did Abebe feel standing outside the flat before the evening began?
qa.a: He was probably a little nervous and careful, never having been to a Jewish home for a festival, which is why he asked Noa beforehand.

qa.q: What did Abebe do that built trust?
qa.a: He asked about customs first, brought suitable sweets, and watched the blessing respectfully without needing to share the beliefs.

qa.q: How did Noa's grandfather see Abebe by the end of the night?
qa.a: He seemed warmly accepting of Abebe, pressing his hand and inviting him back for the eighth night.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who visits a friend's home for their festival, brings sweets and respects customs without sharing the beliefs.
